title: Jumia Food's Last December, Thirteen Months After Its Founders Left
dek: In December 2023 Jumia's new managers closed its food delivery business in seven African markets, a year after the co-founders stepped down.

story.founder: Francis Dufay (chief executive after co-founders Sacha Poignonnec and Jeremy Hodara stepped down in 2022)
story.event: New management closing Jumia Food in seven markets after the co-founders' departure
story.summary: In November 2022 Jumia's co-founders Sacha Poignonnec and Jeremy Hodara stepped down as co-chief executives, and the supervisory board appointed Francis Dufay to cut losses. After cutting about 900 jobs and ending food delivery in three smaller markets, Jumia announced on 14 December 2023 that it would close Jumia Food, about 11% of its gross merchandise value and never profitable, in its seven remaining markets by the end of that month. It went on to leave South Africa and Tunisia in 2024.
paragraphs: On 7 November 2022 Jumia's supervisory board announced that Sacha Poignonnec and Jeremy Hodara were stepping down as co-chief executives. They had founded the e-commerce company in Lagos in 2012 with Tunde Kehinde and Raphael Afaedor, who had left years before, and had taken it onto the New York Stock Exchange in 2019. It had not had a profitable quarter since. In his farewell, Poignonnec thanked those who made "e-commerce, food delivery and digital payments possible", among them "our restaurants, our drivers".

The board gave the job to Francis Dufay, a former McKinsey consultant who had run Jumia's business in Ivory Coast, with Antoine Maillet-Mezeray in charge of finance and operations. Their mandate, in the board's words, was a "clear path to profitability". Before the end of 2022 Jumia cut about 900 jobs, a fifth of its staff, halted Jumia Prime and stopped food delivery in Egypt, Ghana and Senegal, where it was sub-scale.

The rest of the food business was harder to judge. In the third quarter of 2022 it had been the fastest-growing category, with a fifth of items sold, and in the first nine months of 2023 it still made up about 11 per cent of gross merchandise value. But it had never made a profit since it began in 2013, and Dufay pointed to rising competition and costs. On 14 December 2023 Jumia announced that Jumia Food would close in Nigeria, Kenya, Uganda, Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria and Ivory Coast by the end of the month. "We must take the right decision and fully focus our management, our teams and our capital resources," Dufay said. Some of its staff moved to the goods business; a few lost their jobs.

The retreat went on. Operating losses for 2023 fell by 64 per cent, to $73 million. In October 2024 Jumia said it would also leave South Africa and Tunisia, calling it a difficult decision. By 2026, an article on Jumia's own website said, it had left Algeria too, worked in eight countries with fewer than 2,000 staff, against 4,318 at the end of 2022, and was still working towards break-even.

quote.text: 'If it cannot be helped, and one of the remaining two must be dispensed with, which of them should be foregone?' The Master answered, 'Part with the food. From of old, death has been the lot of all men; but if the people have no faith in their rulers, there is no standing for the state.'
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Asked what a ruler should give up when he cannot keep everything, Confucius ranked the people's confidence above even food. Jumia's managers gave up a business worth about a tenth of its sales. Whether they kept the confidence of staff, sellers and investors is a question the loss figures cannot answer.

reflection: Jumia Food was not failing in the obvious way. It was growing, people used it, and it had been part of the founders' picture of the company. It had simply never paid for itself, and the people who had to say so were not the people who had started it.

You will inherit work you did not choose, and some of your own projects will one day be judged by people who were not there when they began. It helps to keep two questions apart: is this growing, and does it carry its own weight? And when something has to end, how the people inside it are told matters as much as the decision.
invitation: Pick one thing you keep doing because it is growing or familiar. Ask yourself plainly whether it repays the time it takes, write the answer down, and do nothing more about it today.

cross_checks.claim: Poignonnec and Hodara stepped down as co-CEOs on 7 November 2022 and the board named Francis Dufay acting CEO.
In late 2022 Jumia cut about 900 jobs, a fifth of its staff.
On 14 December 2023 Jumia announced the closure of Jumia Food in its seven remaining markets by the end of December.
Jumia Food was about 11% of gross merchandise value and had never been profitable.
In 2024 Jumia announced it would leave South Africa and Tunisia.

research_notes: Who decided: the slate listed all four co-founders, but none of them made this decision. Tunde Kehinde and Raphael (Kofi) Afaedor had left years earlier (The Condia says 2014), and Sacha Poignonnec and Jeremy Hodara stepped down as co-CEOs on 7 November 2022. The food exit was decided by the management under Francis Dufay (acting CEO from November 2022) and Antoine Maillet-Mezeray, under a supervisory-board mandate to cut losses; the founder field names Dufay and records the co-founders' departure, and the story says so plainly. The founders are not blamed: the story reports only what the board, the company and the new managers said. Markets: the slate's 'several markets' is the seven-country food closure of December 2023 plus the earlier food exits from Egypt, Ghana and Senegal in late 2022; the country-level exits from South Africa and Tunisia came in 2024 and are told as aftermath. Country is given as Nigeria (Jumia's founding market and the first named in reports); the closure covered seven countries. Figures: food delivery's share is given as about 11% of GMV for the nine months to September 2023 by TechCrunch, TechCabal and Business Daily; TechCrunch's 20% figure is for items sold in Q3 2022, a different measure, and both are reported as such. Job losses: TechCabal (2023) and Nairametrics (2024) both give about 900, or 20%, from the cuts that began in Q4 2022; for the food closure itself the company said some staff would move to the goods business and a few would leave, and no number was published. The 2026 figures (eight markets, fewer than 2,000 staff, 4,318 at the end of 2022) come from an article published on Jumia's own website and are attributed to it. Confucius's answer concerns what a ruler should sacrifice in extremity; it is applied by analogy, and the coincidence of 'food' is not the point of the connection.
